name: Dragon fruit
summary: How Filipino growers, from the big farms of Ilocos and Pangasinan to backyard planters, raise dragon fruit from stem cuttings on posts until the first fruit. It covers the post, the cuttings, training the stems over the top, and picking the fruit in the rainy months.
season: Most farmers plant at the start of the rains, about May to June, so the cuttings root fast. On low or heavy ground some wait until the heaviest rains ease, because wet soil rots new cuttings. Bearing plants flower and fruit through the rainy months, about May to October, with the peak around June to August.
material: Stem cuttings about 30 to 45 cm long from healthy, mature plants that already bear well, cut from older green stems, not soft new tips. The cut end is left to dry in the shade for several days until it seals, so it does not rot. Some farmers first root the cuttings in bags of soil and compost for a few weeks before setting them at the post.
spacing: Posts about 2 to 3 m apart in the row, with about 3 m between rows, a little over 1,100 to about 1,600 posts a hectare. Three to four cuttings around each post. Backyard growers often plant along a fence or wall.
water: Mostly rain fed. Cuttings get light watering until they root, and plants on sandy soil are watered about once a week in long dry spells. Water must never stand around the posts. Raised mounds and canals keep the roots dry in the rains.
fertilizer: Rotted chicken manure and compost are the base, a few kilos per post at planting and every few months. Farmers who buy fertilizer use complete fertilizer (14 14 14) every two to three months, and some give muriate of potash (0 0 60) before flowering for sweeter fruit.
care: Mulching the mounds, hand weeding, tying the young stems up the post, removing low side shoots, cutting the tip at the top so it branches over the ring, and pruning crowded and old branches after each season. Some farmers hand pollinate at night.
harvest: Fruits are cut when the skin is fully colored and the green flaps start turning, about a month after flowering, through the rainy months. Harvest goes every few days in the peak months. The fruit is cut with shears, kept in the shade, packed in crates without stacking too deep, and sold within a few days.

ways.label: Stem cuttings on posts (sanga sa poste)

steps.title: Set up the posts
steps.how: Plant a concrete post, or a strong hardwood or live post, about 1.5 to 2 m above the ground with about half a meter buried, and fix an old tire, a concrete ring or a bamboo frame on top for the branches to hang over. Space posts about 2 to 3 m apart in rows about 3 m apart.
steps.tip: Concrete lasts. Soft wooden posts rot and fall once the plant gets heavy.

parts.title: Cast or buy strong posts
parts.how: Concrete lasts the longest. One Cagayan farm cast its own posts about 5 inches square and 7 feet long, with four iron bars left sticking out of the top to hold the ring.

parts.title: Set them deep and in line
parts.how: Stretch a line along the row and stand each post straight about 2 feet deep in the ground. Many farms set posts about 2 m apart in rows about 2.5 to 3 m apart.

parts.title: Fix the ring on top
parts.how: Slip an old motorcycle or tricycle tire over the iron bars and hold it with two crossing slats of wood or anahaw, so the branches can hang over it later.

steps.title: Make a mound and feed it
steps.how: Around each post, loosen the soil and raise a low mound so rain drains away quickly. Mix in a few kilos of rotted chicken or animal manure or compost.

parts.title: Dig a hole for each cutting
parts.how: Dig about four holes around each post, each about 6 inches out from the post and about 2 feet wide and deep.

parts.title: Fill with a loose, fed mix
parts.how: Fill the holes back with topsoil mixed with old sawdust and dried chicken manure, which holds some water for the new roots but still drains.

parts.title: Heap it toward the post
parts.how: Pile the loose soil a little higher at the post so rain runs off and never stands at the base of the cuttings.

steps.title: Cure the cuttings
steps.how: Cut the stems, trim the bottom end, and lay the cuttings in a shaded, airy place for several days until the cut end dries and seals.

parts.title: Take stems from good plants
parts.how: Cut from plants that bear well and show no stem rot, or buy from a farm you trust, since sick cuttings carry the disease into a new field. Use mature green stems, not soft new tips.

parts.title: Cut pieces to length
parts.how: Farms here plant pieces about 8 to 12 inches long, and some use longer ones. Cut the bottom end at a slant so you know which end goes into the soil.

parts.title: Dry the cut end in the shade
parts.how: Lay the pieces in a dry, shaded, airy spot for about a week, until the cut end dries and closes over. Many growers dip the cut end in a fungicide first.

parts.title: Or root them in bags first
parts.how: Some farmers set the cured pieces in bags of soil and compost for a few weeks and move them to the post only once they have rooted.

steps.title: Plant three or four cuttings a post
steps.how: Set three or four cuttings around each post, the flat side against it, burying only the lower few centimeters, and tie each one loosely to the post with soft string or cloth strips. Water lightly once.
steps.tip: Plant the cutting the right way up: the end that was nearer the mother plant goes into the soil.

parts.title: Plant them shallow and leaning
parts.how: Set each cured piece about 3 inches deep in its hole, leaning in so its flat side rests against one face of the post.

parts.title: Tie each one on
parts.how: Tie the cutting loosely to the post with soft string, cloth strips or plastic straw so wind cannot rock it while it roots.

parts.title: Water only a little
parts.how: In soil with some clay the cuttings need very little water while they root. New growth usually shows after about two weeks.

steps.title: Mulch the mound
steps.how: Cover the mound with rice straw, rice hull or dry grass to keep the soil damp and cool and the weeds down.

steps.title: Water sparingly until rooted
steps.how: Water once or twice a week if no rain falls, only enough to keep the soil slightly moist. The cuttings root in a few weeks. Soggy soil makes them turn soft and yellow.

steps.title: Replace the ones that rotted
steps.how: Pull out cuttings that turned soft, yellow or black at the base and plant fresh cured ones in their place.

steps.title: Tie the stem up the post
steps.how: Keep one or two strong shoots per cutting and tie them to the post every so often as they climb. Break off the side shoots that come out low on the stem.

steps.title: Feed every few months
steps.how: Every two to three months, spread compost or chicken manure around the mound, and farmers who buy fertilizer add a small amount of complete fertilizer (14 14 14) away from the stems.

steps.title: Weed the mounds
steps.how: Pull weeds by hand around the posts, since the roots are shallow and a hoe cuts them. Slash the grass between rows.

steps.title: Cut the tip at the top
steps.how: When the stem passes the ring on top, cut its tip so it branches out. Guide the new branches over the ring so they hang down on all sides, which is where the flowers come.

steps.title: Watch the night flowers
steps.how: Flowers open at night and last only one night. Some farmers dust pollen from one flower onto another with a soft brush at night or early morning, which helps fruit set, especially on types that do not set well alone. Look out for ants, mealybugs and stem rot.

steps.title: Pick the fully colored fruit
steps.how: The first real harvest comes at about 18 months, though some plants fruit at 12. Fruit is ready about a month after the flower opens, when the skin turns fully red or pink and the green flaps start to change color at the tips. Cut it off with shears, leaving a short stalk.
steps.tip: Handle gently and keep in the shade. Bruised fruit spoils fast.

steps.title: Prune after the season
steps.how: After the last fruit of the season, cut out old, crowded, broken and diseased branches, keeping the healthy young ones that hang down. Burn or bury rotten stems away from the field.

ways.note: Cuttings usually give their first fruit at about 12 to 18 months. We count the first real harvest at 18 months (540 days).

mistakes: Planting in low spots where water stands, so the stems rot at the base.
Planting fresh cuttings without curing the cut end.
Using soft wooden posts that rot and fall under the weight.
Letting every side shoot grow, so the plant never reaches the top or flowers late.
Picking the fruit before it is fully colored, so it stays sour.
better: Plant cuttings from a high yielding, self fruiting variety, and mix varieties for better fruit set.
Use concrete posts with a ring on top and raised beds with good drainage.
Test the soil and feed by the result, with more potash before flowering.
Hand pollinate at night when bees and moths are few, and keep pruning after every season.
Scout weekly for ants, mealybugs, stem rot and fruit rot, and use integrated pest management.
Some growers light the field at night in the cool months to get fruit out of season. Ask experienced growers before trying it.

watering.traditional: Dragon fruit here is mostly rain fed: cuttings get a light watering until they root, and growers on sandy soil water about once a week by can or hose in long dry spells. Most of the work goes into keeping water away, with mounds around each post and canals between the rows.
watering.method: A watering can or hose on the mound around each post on small farms, and drip lines with an emitter at each post on bigger farms in the drier provinces. Water early in the morning, on the mound and not over the stems.
watering.rainfed: Plant as the rains begin, on a raised mound around each post, and keep it covered with rice straw, rice hull or dry grass so the soil stays cool and damp. The plant stores water in its stems and lives through the dry months on rain alone, but it bears less. The flowers come with the rains, from about May to October, so rain fed plants still give a fair crop.
watering.dryseason: Plants not in flower: about every two weeks, or once a week on sandy soil. Plants in flower or with fruit: twice a week in a dry spell. Feel the mound and water when it is dry a finger deep, or when the stems start to look thin and wrinkled.
watering.wet: Never let water stand around the posts: raise the mounds, dig canals between the rows and keep them open. Too much rain drops flowers and rots fruit, and soft rot of the stems spreads in wet weather, so cut out and bury rotten stems away from the field.

schedule.often: No water. Keep them dry in an airy, shaded place
schedule.why: The cut end has to dry and seal or it rots in the soil.

schedule.often: Water lightly once at planting, then once or twice a week if no rain falls, letting the mound dry a little in between
schedule.amount: A light sprinkle on the mound, never a soaking
schedule.why: Cuttings without roots turn soft and yellow in wet soil.

schedule.often: About once a week in dry weather. Skip it when it rains
schedule.amount: One to two watering cans a post, enough to wet the mound without making it soggy
schedule.why: Steady growth now gives a thick stem that reaches the ring sooner.

schedule.often: About once a week in dry spells, every two weeks in cooler weeks
schedule.amount: One to two watering cans a post
schedule.why: The hanging branches grown now carry next season's flowers.

schedule.often: Many growers hold back water for a few weeks before the flowering season
schedule.amount: None, unless the stems shrivel badly
schedule.why: A dry spell before the season brings out more flower buds.

schedule.often: Twice a week in dry spells, once a week when some rain falls, keeping the mound evenly moist
schedule.amount: About 2 to 4 watering cans (20 to 40 liters) a post a week, split into two waterings
schedule.why: Even moisture gives big fruits. A dry spell then a heavy soaking splits them.

schedule.stage: After the season, pruning and rest
schedule.often: About every two weeks in dry months, not at all in the rains
schedule.amount: One to two watering cans a post
schedule.why: The plant only needs enough to keep the new branches growing.

critical: From the first flower buds to harvest, about a month after each flower opens, when a dry spell drops buds and gives small or split fruit.
The first months after the cuttings root, when young shoots shrivel and stop climbing in long dry weather.

signs.dry: Stems turn thin, flat and wrinkled and lose their color, new shoots stop, and flower buds dry and fall.
signs.wet: Stems turn soft and yellow, then brown or black from the base. Roots rot. Flowers drop. And fruits split or rot.

better: A drip line with an emitter at each post, run twice a week through flowering and fruit growth in dry spells, keeps the moisture even, gives bigger fruit and stops splitting.
Hold water back for a few weeks before the flowering season, then water steadily once the buds show.
